body_html:
If you hold a national driving licence from an ASEAN member state and want to rent a motorbike in Hanoi, here is the position the official documents support. Vietnam is a party to the 1985 ASEAN agreement that recognises domestic driving licences from other member states for visitors on a temporary stay. Vietnam's 2025 licensing circular from the Ministry of Public Security says a foreign national licence normally has to be exchanged for a Vietnamese one, but that an international treaty Vietnam has joined takes precedence where it says otherwise. The US Embassy in Hanoi, meanwhile, describes ASEAN recognition as applying only "in certain circumstances" and still advises getting a Vietnamese licence. So an ASEAN driving licence for a Vietnam motorbike rental sits in a stronger position than most other foreign licences, but it only helps when it is valid, in English or certified-translated, and covers the motorcycle class you intend to ride. Below is what each source actually says and which documents a renter should carry on the bike.

What the ASEAN licence agreement actually says

The treaty behind the "ASEAN licence" idea is the Agreement on the Recognition of Domestic Driving Licences Issued by ASEAN Countries, signed in Kuala Lumpur on 9 July 1985. Its first article commits the contracting parties to recognise all domestic driving licences issued by the designated authorities or national automobile associations of ASEAN countries, with one explicit exclusion: temporary, provisional and learner's licences are not covered.

Article 2 sets the scope that matters to a tourist. Holders of a licence issued in one ASEAN country who intend to make "only a temporary stay" in another ASEAN country may drive there the classes or types of vehicle their licence permits. Three further articles narrow that promise in ways renters often miss:

  • Language (Article 3): a licence not drawn up in English must be accompanied by a certified English translation.
  • Validity (Article 4): a licence that is invalid under the issuing country's law, or that has expired, is not recognised at all.
  • Local rules still apply (Articles 5 and 6): recognition does not excuse the holder from meeting the driving standards of the host country, and holders are liable for traffic-offence penalties under the host country's law.

The agreement's annexes list licence classes for the six original signatories (Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand). According to the ASEAN Secretariat's treaty record, the agreement entered into force on 7 January 1988, Viet Nam acceded on 22 January 1997, and the parties now also include Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar and, since 24 November 2025, Timor-Leste. In other words, every current ASEAN member state has signed up, so a Thai, Malaysian, Singaporean, Indonesian, Filipino, Bruneian, Cambodian, Lao, Myanmar or Timorese national licence falls within the treaty's text.

How Vietnam's 2025 licensing circular treats a foreign licence

Driver licensing in Vietnam moved under the Ministry of Public Security in 2025, and the operative instrument is Circular 12/2025/TT-BCA. The full text published on the Government's policy portal contains the two clauses that decide an ASEAN rider's position. Article 18 says that a foreigner who wants to drive in Vietnam and holds a national licence must go through the procedure to exchange it for the corresponding Vietnamese licence. The very next point adds that where an international treaty on driving licences to which Vietnam is a party provides otherwise, the treaty's provisions apply.

Read together with the ASEAN agreement, that is the legal basis for saying an ASEAN national licence can be used by a visitor on a temporary stay without exchange. It is also why the recognition is narrower than many blog posts suggest: the treaty, not the circular, defines who benefits, and the treaty only speaks of temporary stays, valid non-provisional licences, and English text or a certified translation.

Two things the circular says about international driving permits

The same circular is blunt about IDPs. An IDP issued by Vietnam under the 1968 Convention on Road Traffic has no validity inside Vietnamese territory, and IDPs recognised under a treaty Vietnam has joined are handled according to that treaty. It also lists what cannot be exchanged for a Vietnamese licence: temporary foreign licences, international driving permits, expired or damaged licences, and licences not issued by a competent authority. If your only motorcycle entitlement is a learner or provisional licence from home, neither the ASEAN agreement nor the exchange route will help you.

Why the US Embassy still recommends a Vietnamese licence

The US Embassy and Consulate page on driving in Vietnam states that foreign driver licences, even when accompanied by an international driving permit, are not valid in Vietnam. It then acknowledges that a licence from an ASEAN country "may be recognized in certain circumstances", before advising readers to obtain a local Vietnamese licence if they wish to drive legally. The embassy does not spell out what those circumstances are, which is exactly why the treaty text above matters.

The practical reading for a renter is cautious. The treaty gives you a defensible document for a short visit, but the embassy's wording signals that officials, insurers and rental counters do not all apply it the same way. If you are staying for months rather than weeks, the embassy's advice to convert to a Vietnamese licence aligns with the circular, which reserves exchange for foreigners holding a diplomatic or official identity card, or a temporary or permanent residence card valid for three months or more. Our guide to preparing documents for a foreign licence exchange in Hanoi walks through that route for long-term renters.

What the embassy says the exchange involves

For anyone eligible, the embassy page lists the usual file: an application form for exchanging a motor vehicle driving licence; authenticated copies of the foreign licence with a notarised Vietnamese translation; copies of the passport biodata page, the Vietnamese visa page and the residency permit (two copies of each); a valid health check unless the licence's validity will simply follow the visa or residence permit; a photograph taken at the police office; and 135,000 VND in cash for the application fee, with translation, photo or delivery costs extra. The embassy flags the list as non-exhaustive, directs applicants to the nearest Traffic Police Department or commune-level police, and notes that the online portal at dichvucong.gov.vn is in Vietnamese only.

What to carry on the bike as an ASEAN licence holder

Because recognition depends on the licence itself being in order, the documents you carry decide whether the treaty protects you at a roadside stop. Put these together before you leave home:

  • Your original, in-date national licence showing a motorcycle class, not a car-only entitlement. The treaty only lets you ride the classes the licence permits, and an expired card is not recognised.
  • A certified English translation if the licence is not printed in English. Several ASEAN licences carry both the national language and English; check yours before you fly.
  • Photo ID at all times. UK travel advice notes that you must always carry photographic ID in Vietnam, and that the authorities accept a printed copy of the passport photo page and visa. Carry the copies and leave the passport locked up.
  • Proof of third-party insurance for the motorbike. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office says it is illegal to drive in Vietnam without it; ask the rental shop which certificate stays with the bike.

Two further points from the GOV.UK Vietnam safety and security page apply to every rider, ASEAN licence or not. First, the UK advice is that its own nationals need both the 1968 version of the international driving permit and their UK licence while driving a car or motorbike in Vietnam; if you hold a non-ASEAN licence, that pairing is the route to check, and our article on checking the motorcycle category on a 1968 Convention IDP explains what to look for. Second, the FCDO tells travellers not to use a passport as a deposit for hiring a vehicle or as a guarantee for paying a traffic fine, and warns that a rental shop holding your passport can keep it against claimed damage.

What Hanoi rental shops are likely to ask for

None of the official documents above tells a rental shop what to check, so counter practice varies. What the sources do establish is the shape of a sensible conversation. A shop that takes licensing seriously will want to see the licence itself and confirm it shows a motorcycle class, because the treaty ties recognition to the class on the card. It may ask for an English translation if the card is in Thai, Khmer, Lao, Burmese or Bahasa only, mirroring Article 3 of the agreement. It should be able to tell you what third-party insurance paper accompanies the bike. And, following the UK advice, you can reasonably decline to leave your passport behind; our note on passport security during a Hanoi motorbike rental lists safer alternatives to discuss.

If you plan to rent from Thuê xe máy Nguyễn Hà at Ngõ 5 Nguyễn Văn Cừ, Bồ Đề, Long Biên, Hà Nội, the hotline is 0334 699 969 and the shop is open 09:00 to 21:00 daily. Calling ahead to say which ASEAN country issued your licence, what class it shows and whether it is in English lets the shop tell you exactly what to bring. Do not expect any shop to vouch for how a traffic officer will treat your licence; that decision is made at the roadside under Vietnamese law, which Article 6 of the agreement expressly preserves.

Riding conditions the licence does not change

The GOV.UK page describes motorbike travel in Vietnam as much riskier than at home, notes that accidents have killed and injured British nationals, and advises against hiring a motorbike if you are not an experienced rider. Its checklist is short: check the bike thoroughly, rent from a reputable organisation, and wear a good helmet, because riding without one is illegal for riders and passengers. The same page warns that any alcohol in your system can bring a fine and possible imprisonment, and that a foreign national involved in an accident can face criminal charges, compensation claims and a travel ban while police investigate. A recognised licence is a precondition for riding legally, not a shield against any of that, which is why it is worth confirming your cover using our questions to ask your insurer about rental motorbikes in Vietnam.

Frequently asked questions

Which ASEAN licences does the agreement cover?

The ASEAN Secretariat's treaty record lists all eleven member states as parties: Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste and Viet Nam. The agreement excludes temporary, provisional and learner's licences from every country.

Do I also need an international driving permit with an ASEAN licence?

The agreement does not mention an IDP; it works from the domestic licence plus an English translation where needed. Vietnam's circular says IDPs recognised under a treaty Vietnam has joined are applied per that treaty, and UK advice tells British riders to carry a 1968 IDP with their national licence. Carrying a 1968 IDP alongside an ASEAN licence does no harm, but the licence, its class and its validity are what the treaty examines.

Can I use an ASEAN licence if I live in Vietnam?

The treaty speaks only of a temporary stay. Vietnam's circular expects foreigners who reside, work or study in the country, and who hold a residence card or official identity card valid for three months or more, to exchange their national licence for a Vietnamese one. The US Embassy's advice to obtain a local licence is aimed at exactly this group.

Does recognition cover any motorbike size?

No. Article 2 limits you to the classes or types of vehicle your home licence permits. If your card covers only small-capacity motorcycles, that limit travels with you.

Can the rental shop confirm my licence is accepted by the police?

No shop can give that assurance, and the embassy's "certain circumstances" wording shows why. Bring the original licence, a certified English translation if needed, printed passport and visa copies, and the bike's insurance paper, and ride within the class your licence allows.

title: Riding in Vietnam on an ASEAN Motorbike Licence: Recognition Limits and What Hanoi Shops Ask For
